group.passage: People knew how to make pictures with light long before they knew how to keep them. Even in Aristotle's time, it was understood that light entering a dark room through a tiny hole would project an image of the outside world onto the opposite wall. This device, later named the camera obscura, may have helped some painters plan their work, but its images vanished the moment the light changed. Around 1800, an Englishman laid leaves on paper treated with silver, yet he too failed to stop his images from fading away. A Frenchman, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, spent about ten years working on this problem. In 1826 or 1827, he coated a metal plate with bitumen, a natural tar that hardens where light falls on it, and placed it inside a camera obscura facing an upstairs window of his country house. Then he waited. Accounts of the wait range from about eight hours to several days. The result, a dim view of rooftops and a courtyard, is the oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera. In 1829, Niépce teamed up with Louis Daguerre, a Paris showman, and after Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre carried on alone. His method used a copper plate coated with silver, and mercury vapor made the image appear. Daguerre had hoped to sell his secret, but the French government gave him a yearly payment instead and made the method free for everyone. It was announced to the public in 1839. The daguerreotype spread quickly. At first, people had to sit still for about twenty minutes, but better chemicals and mirrors soon cut the time to under a minute. By 1850, American studios were producing more than three million pictures a year. Still, every plate was the only one of its kind, since the process made no negative from which copies could be printed. By 1860, paper prints made from glass negatives had replaced it. Niépce's plate, meanwhile, lay forgotten for decades until a historian tracked it down in 1952. Today it rests in a sealed case in Texas, a quiet reminder of how much patience a single early picture once required.

1.strategy_zh: 主旨題先找每一段的重點：起源（留不住影像）→ 突破（尼埃普、達蓋爾）→ 流行與被取代 → 底片下落。正確選項要能涵蓋「開始」和「之後的興衰」兩個階段，只講一段的選項要排除。

translation_zh.text:
早在人們懂得如何把影像留住之前，就已經知道怎麼用光做出影像。甚至在亞里斯多德的時代，人們就明白：光線穿過小孔進入暗室，會把外面世界的影像投射到對面的牆上。這種後來被稱為「暗箱」的裝置，或許幫助過一些畫家構圖，但光線一變，它的影像就消失無蹤。大約 1800 年，一位英國人把葉子放在塗了銀的紙上，但他同樣無法阻止影像褪去。

法國人約瑟夫‧尼塞福爾‧尼埃普花了大約十年研究這個問題。1826 或 1827 年，他在一塊金屬板上塗了瀝青——一種遇光就會變硬的天然焦油——然後把它放進一個對著自家鄉間住宅樓上窗戶的暗箱裡。接著他就開始等待。關於他等了多久，說法從大約八小時到好幾天都有。成果是一幅模糊的屋頂與庭院景象，也是現存最古老、用相機拍攝的照片。

1829 年，尼埃普與巴黎的表演經營者路易‧達蓋爾合作；1833 年尼埃普過世後，達蓋爾獨自繼續研究。他的方法使用鍍銀的銅板，再以水銀蒸氣讓影像顯現。達蓋爾原本希望出售他的祕方，但法國政府改為每年支付他一筆款項，並讓所有人都能免費使用這個方法。這個方法在 1839 年向大眾公開。

銀版攝影法迅速流行。起初，人們得坐著不動約二十分鐘，但更好的化學藥劑和鏡子很快就把時間縮短到一分鐘以內。到了 1850 年，美國的照相館每年拍出超過三百萬張照片。不過，每一塊銀版都是獨一無二的，因為這個方法不產生可以用來印出副本的負片。到了 1860 年，用玻璃負片印出的紙本照片已經取代了它。

至於尼埃普的那塊金屬板，則被遺忘了數十年，直到 1952 年才被一位歷史學家找到。如今它靜靜地存放在德州的一個密封箱裡，提醒人們早年拍一張照片曾經需要多大的耐心。

open_tasks.prompt: Today we can take a photo in less than a second and copy it as many times as we like. Do you think this makes each photo less special than a daguerreotype was? Answer in one or two English sentences and give a reason.
reference_answers: Yes, I think so, because a daguerreotype could not be copied, so each one was a rare and precious object.
Not really, because a photo is special when it reminds us of a person or a moment, no matter how easy it was to take.
